abstract.title: Summary
abstract.p: A challenge in treating glioblastoma (GBM) is its phenotypic heterogeneity between patients and within tumors. Chlorotoxin (CLTX), a peptide from scorpion venom, broadly binds glioma cells through a mechanism involving surface matrix metalloproteinase-2 (MMP-2). We previously developed chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells incorporating CLTX as the GBM recognition domain. Here, we report interim clinical experience of a phase 1 trial evaluating intracavity/intratumoral (ICT) delivery of CLTX-CAR T cells in four patients with MMP-2-expressing recurrent GBM (NCT04214392), with the primary objectives of feasibility and safety. The therapy is well tolerated with no dose-limiting toxicities. Three of the four participants (75%) exhibit a best response of stable disease. CLTX-CAR T cells are detected in the tumor cavity fluid and at lower levels in the blood. Human anti-CAR antibody assays do not detect humoral immunogenicity against the CLTX-CAR. These observations support further clinical evaluation of CLTX-CAR therapy.

abstract.p: Chlorotoxin peptide-directed CAR T cells represent a distinct class of tumor-targeting immunotherapy. In this interim clinical trial report, Barish et al. show feasibility and tolerability in glioblastoma, with early indications of bioactivity. These findings support further development of this and other toxin-based CAR platforms for targeting solid tumors.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Glioblastoma (GBM; isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH)-wild-type World Health Organization [WHO] grade 4) is the most aggressive brain neoplasm. Despite advances in multimodal therapy including surgical excision, radiation, chemotherapy, electric fields, and immunotherapy, GBM remains uniformly lethal.1 Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell immunotherapy is being explored as a strategy to improve GBM outcomes and has demonstrated early promise in improving responses and patient survival.2,3 However, the overall response rates and the durability of responses following GBM-targeted CAR T cells remain unacceptably low, especially when compared to the remarkable clinical responses observed with hematological malignancies (reviewed in Goyco et al. and Song et al.4,5).

Solid tumors such as GBM are highly plastic and heterogeneous, lacking the widely expressed target antigens characteristic of hematologic cancers.6,7 Immune evasion remains a major barrier to CAR T cell therapy,8 as tumor cell populations can downregulate, sequester, or mutate targeted antigens (clonal evolution), or minor pre-existing antigen-negative populations can expand to occupy the space vacated by targeted tumor cells (clonal expansion).9,10,11,12

Some years ago, Sontheimer and coworkers demonstrated that chlorotoxin (CLTX), a 36-amino acid peptide toxin component of scorpion venom, selectively binds to the cell membranes of glioma cells spanning all malignancy grades, as well as other neuroectodermal tumors, but not to non-malignant brain cells or other somatic cells.13,14 This critical observation has been confirmed in clinical trials employing CLTX as a vehicle for tumoricidal or imaging agents, and these clinical trials have demonstrated that the CLTX peptide itself is well tolerated by patients.15,16 Recently, Olson et al. have shown that a fluorescent CLTX biconjugate (CLTX:Cy5.5) can be used to selectively “paint” glioma cells for surgical resection while leaving adjacent brain cells non-fluorescent.17,18,19,20,21 This fine discrimination between cancerous and normal cells is consistent with the original observations of Soroceanu et al. and Lyons et al.13,14 and highlights the widespread yet highly selective binding of CLTX to glioma cells.

We have recently developed a distinct class of toxin-based CAR T cells employing CLTX as the tumor recognition domain and thereby directing T cells to effectively recognize and kill glioma cells in preclinical studies.22 This use of a peptide toxin for this purpose has shown that CLTX-CAR T cells bind and kill a wide range of patient-derived glioma cells, while not exhibiting off-target recognition of normal cells in the brain or other organs, highlighting the potential clinical utility of CLTX-CAR T cells.22

Based on these observations, we initiated a phase 1 clinical trial of CLTX-CAR T cells as a therapy for patients with recurrent or refractory GBM and IDH-mutant astrocytoma, grade 4 (NCT04214392). With the overall goal of evaluating safety and feasibility, we report here our interim observations from an initial patient cohort receiving multiple and escalating doses of CLTX-CAR T cells delivered to the tumor resection cavity (ICT administration).

sec.title: Study design and patient characteristics
sec.p: This first-in-human phase 1 dose escalation clinical trial (NCT04214392) was approved by the protocol review committee of the City of Hope National Medical Center, and written consent for treatment was obtained for leukapheresis and treatment. This trial enrolled heavily pretreated patients with no enrollment restrictions for tumor size, multi-focality, or number of recurrences (Table 1). Four participants with histopathologically verified recurrent GBM, three female and one male, ages 40 to 58 years (median 56), were enrolled as part of a safety lead-in cohort and received CLTX-CAR T cells intratumorally. All had completed standard-of-care therapy, including tumor resection, radiation, and chemotherapy, and were enrolled following documented radiographic progression based on ≥20% moderate/high tumor metalloproteinase-2 (MMP-2) expression and a Karnofsky performance status (KPS) of ≥80. Patient characteristics along with other clinical and histopathological parameters are detailed in Table 1.

sec.p: CLTX-CAR T cells were manufactured from enriched CD62L + central memory, stem cell memory, and naive T cell subsets (Tn/mem) as previously employed by our group in other CAR T cell trials.2,23 Phenotypic analysis revealed that the CLTX-CAR T cells exhibit a balanced proportion of CD4+ and CD8+ subsets, with high proportions of T cells expressing the memory markers CD27 and CD62L and low expression of the senescence markers CD57, PD-1, and TIM-3 (Figure S1). The median time from apheresis to surgery and catheter placement was 50 days (min 0; max 90), and the median time from surgery and catheter placement to the first CAR T cell infusion (C1) was 19 days (min 8, max 55). Unique patient number (UPN) 502 experienced the longest delay from apheresis to surgery (90 days) due to intractable seizures and contracting COVID. This patient also required 4 weeks of post-operative rehabilitation before starting CAR T cell treatment, in contrast to the other three participants, who started their CAR T cell treatment within 1 month after surgery. CAR T cell treatment consisted of three weekly infusions of CLTX-CAR T cells at a dose schedule of 4, 20, and 20 × 106 CAR+ cells directly into the tumor resection cavity via an implanted Rickham catheter (Figures 1A and 1B). Patients were then further evaluated for 1 week after the third infusion for dose-limiting toxicities (DLTs) (Figure 1A). Additional intracavity/intratumoral (ICT) infusions of up to 20 × 106 CLTX-CAR T cells were allowed, and patients were followed for toxicities, disease responses, and survival.

sec.title: MMP-2 expression as an enrollment criterion
sec.p: Given the association of MMP-2 expression with CLTX binding,22,24,25 we used MMP-2 immunoreactivity in patient biopsies as a marker for CLTX-CAR T cell targetability, and thus as an eligibility criterion for patient enrollment. As proof of concept, a tissue microarray containing formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) specimens of multiple astrocytic gliomas (WHO grade 1–4) from patients of different ages and gender was stained with MMP-2-specific antibody and with biotin-conjugated CLTX (CLTX:biotin). As depicted in Figure S2A, parallel increases in MMP-2 immunoreactivity and CLTX:biotin binding were associated with higher WHO grades,26 an association that was maintained regardless of patient age or gender (Figure S2B). Importantly, normal brain tissue did not exhibit either MMP-2 immunoreactivity or CLTX:biotin binding (Figures S2C and S3), nor did normal breast, colon, and skin tissues (Figure S3). These observations indicated that MMP-2 immunoreactivity in patient tumor specimens could be used as an enrollment criterion for this trial. Accordingly, immunohistochemical staining for MMP-2 on patient FFPE tissues was evaluated by a neuropathologist. Patients with MMP-2 expression scores greater than 20% (moderate and/or high expression staining [2+/3+]) were considered eligible for inclusion in this trial, with the expectation that this criterion would be sufficiently stringent to limit enrollment to research participants with the potential to achieve therapeutic benefit from CLTX-CAR T cell therapy. Baseline MMP-2 expression was established at the time of enrollment from the most recent archived tumor tissue (Figure 1C; enrollment). It was also evaluated on pre-treatment tumor tissue obtained at time of catheter placement (Figure 1C; pre-treatment). Immunofluorescence (IF) evaluation of the biopsies also revealed prominent MMP-2 expression and CLTX binding on both tumor cells and, in some samples, intratumoral vasculature, observations together indicating the potential targetability of MMP-2-expressing GBM by CLTX-CAR T cells (Figure 1C).

sec.title: Toxicity
sec.p: Five participants were enrolled on the trial and underwent surgical resection of their recurrent GBM (Figure 1D). However, due to complications from the surgery, one patient required a protocol-disallowed treatment (a ventriculoperitoneal shunt) and did not receive CAR T cells (Figure 1D). The remaining four research participants received at least three weekly infusions of CLTX-CAR T cells, received at least 80% of the proposed dose of CLTX-CAR T cells at each cycle, and were monitored through the rest period until completion of the 28-day DLT evaluation period (Figure 1D). They were thus evaluable for dose escalation and response evaluation. None of these participants experienced a DLT (DLT rate 0, 90% confidence interval [CI] [0,0.53]). There were no central nervous system (CNS) events attributed as probable or definite to CLTX-CAR T cells of grade 3 or higher and no cytokine release syndrome (CRS) events. The most common adverse event (AE) was grade 2 hypertension, and it was experienced by 3 participants (Table 2). There were no grade 4 or 5 AEs at least possibly attributed to CAR T cells. Two participants experienced grade 3 cerebral edema, one of which was a serious AE requiring hospitalization that was possibly attributed to the CLTX-CAR T cells (Table 2). Grade 3 AEs were only considered DLTs if they were attributed at a probable or higher level.

sec.title: Clinical outcomes after CLTX-CAR T cell administration
sec.p: Per study protocol and clinical standards, treatment responses to CLTX-CAR T cell infusion were evaluated by magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Research participants underwent MRI at the time of enrollment (pre-operative), before CLTX-CAR T treatment (post-operative), and 1 week after the third treatment cycle at the end of the 28-day DLT evaluation period. Participants tolerating CLTX-CAR T cell treatment were evaluated for eligibility to receive optional cycles after completing the DLT evaluation period and received additional MRI scans. The clinicopathologic observations indicate that three of the four participants achieved transient stable disease after three cycles of CLTX-CAR T cell treatment (UPNs 479, 487, and 502), for an overall disease control rate (DCR) of 75% with 90% CI [0.25, 0.99], as illustrated in Figure 2A. However, ultimately, all four participants died of disease progression, with three participants surviving less than 6 months and one participant (90% CI [0,0.53]) surviving more than 20 months from the time of trial surgery. The MRI scans for UPN 487 demonstrated regional control with no evidence of tumor recurrence at the site of CLTX-CAR T cell infusion in the resected tumor cavity at completion of the DLT period, as well as after 7 cycles (9 weeks post-treatment). However, the tumor did progress at a distant site (Figure 2B). MMP-2 IHC evaluation of this progressive tumor (H score 170 + V2, Figure S4) suggests there was not loss of target antigen expression.

sec.title: Persistence and peripheral trafficking of CLTX-CAR T cells
sec.p: Persistence of CLTX-CAR T cells, a secondary objective of this trial, was monitored in the tumor cavity fluid (TCF) and blood over time. Increases in both total CD3+ T cells and administered CD3+ CLTX-CAR+ T cells as determined by flow cytometry were observed in the TCF following each CAR T cell infusion (Figure 3A). Numbers of CAR+ cells within the total CD3+ T cell population reached their highest levels at cycles 4, 6, and 3 for UPNs 479, 487, and 522, respectively. CLTX-CAR T cells were also detected by qPCR in the peripheral blood of all participants at different times (Figure 3B), indicating that ICT-delivered CLTX-CAR T cells can traffic to the periphery, as was previously observed with IL13Rα2-CAR T cells.2 Interestingly, there was a late spike in peripheral CLTX-CAR T cells in UPN 487 after resection of the distant recurrent tumor, possibly due to increased leakage of cells from the CNS to the blood with the procedure.

sec.title: Locoregional spikes in inflammatory cytokines after CLTX-CAR T cell administration
sec.p: We previously reported that IL13Rα2-CAR T cell administration induced locoregional spikes of inflammatory cytokines in participants with recurrent high-grade glioma.2 Treatment-related cytokine dynamics were similarly explored in the available TCF and serum samples of participants treated with CLTX-CAR T cells. Low-dimensional visual representation of the 30 evaluated cytokines revealed the same basic distribution patterns between the two trials with regards to compartment (TCF or serum) or day (Figure 4A). Furthermore, qualitative evaluation of cytokine fold changes revealed infusion dependent increases (CxD1) for several cytokines in the TCF of UPNs 479 and 487 (Figure 4B; Tables S1 and S2). Specifically, interferon (IFN)γ-pathway and Th1 immune stimulatory cytokines, including IFNγ, IL-2R, tumor necrosis factor alpha, CXCL9, and CXCL10, were induced in the TCF following treatment. This pattern of cytokine fold changes in the TCF was not observed in UPN 522 (Figure 4B; Table S3), possibly due to the high baseline values in this patient (e.g., CXCL9 and CXCL10, Figure S5). Unfortunately, no TCF samples were collected from UPN 502. Interestingly, lower treatment-dependent changes in cytokine levels were observed in the serum of all four participants (Figure S6; Tables S4–S7) similar to our previous IL13Rα2-CAR T cell trial in GBM,2 reflecting a lack of systemic inflammatory responses after ICT delivery of CLTX-CAR T cells.

sec.title: Evaluation of CLTX-CAR T cell immunogenicity
sec.p: As the non-human CLTX peptide is incorporated in our CAR design, raising the potential risk of immunogenicity, we developed an assay for detecting human anti-CAR antibody (HACA) responses. As depicted in Figure 5A, the HACA assay uses a fluorochrome-conjugated anti-human immunoglobulin (Ig)G1 Fc antibody to detect IgG1 binding to CAR-expressing Jurkat human T cells via flow cytometry. Because the truncated CD19 (CD19t) marker is constitutively expressed in parallel with the CAR in transduced cells, the assay was optimized, and its sensitivity was assessed using a biosimilar fully humanized anti-CD19 IgG1 antibody. The threshold for HACA assay positivity was determined by testing pre-CAR T treatment participant samples (n = 22) for antibody reactivity against CAR-engineered versus unengineered Jurkat cells. Taking these pre-treatment samples to be true negatives, it was established that a mean fluorescence intensity (MFI) fold change of ≥1.3 gives a test with an estimated specificity of 99%. A dilution series (0–10 μg/mL) of the anti-CD19 IgG1 was used to stain Jurkat cells that had been either mock-transduced or transduced with the CLTX(EQ)28Z-T2A-CD19t_epHIV7 vector used in this trial, and the binding of the secondary anti-IgG1 antibody was measured by flow cytometry (Figure 5B). Our analysis suggested a detection threshold of 0.0137 μg/mL of IgG1 bound to CLTX-CAR T cells (Figure 5C). Results of the HACA assay with samples (TCF and serum) from the four participants indicated that no immune reactivity against the CLTX-CAR T cells was detected (Figure 5D).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Here, we report our interim clinical experience and correlative assessments of research participants enrolled on a phase 1 trial evaluating the feasibility and safety of CLTX-CAR T cells after tumor resection. Our initial clinical experience with the first cohort of four participants diagnosed with recurrent GBM and treated with ICT-delivered CLTX-CAR T cells provides evidence that the therapy is both feasible and well tolerated. These clinical findings are significant as they report use of a CAR-directed cellular immunotherapy platform exploiting the target tissue specificity of a peptide toxin. While several recent clinical studies from our group and others have demonstrated safety and clinical benefit mediated by CAR T cells targeting GBM tumor antigens B7H3,27 EGFRvIII,11,28 GD2,29 HER2,30,31 and IL13Ra2,2 GBM remains an aggressive and refractory brain cancer. The study presented here extends clinical experience with GBM-targeted immunotherapies to report on a GBM-targeted CAR employing the CLTX peptide as a tumor recognition domain.

CLTX was an advantageous choice for this study incorporating a venom-derived toxin in a cell-based immunotherapy. The CLTX peptide was originally purified as a component of scorpion venom in the mid-1990s based on its inhibition of a chloride channel (CCl-3) expressed by glioma cells.32,33,34 Subsequent studies with 125I-labeled CLTX indicated binding restricted to glioma and other neuroepithelial tumors but not normal brain and other tissues13,14 and suggested CLTX’s diagnostic and therapeutic potential. Subsequent studies have confirmed the specificity of CLTX binding to tumor tissues and the value of utilizing conjugated CLTX as a research and clinical tool.35

CLTX binding to GBM and other tumor cells is reported to involve a cell surface multimolecular complex involving MMP-2, although the precise nature of the CLTX receptor is the subject of active investigation.22,24,25 We and others find strong concordance between MMP-2 expression and CLTX binding on glioma cells,22,36 and here we demonstrate increased expression on glioma tissues of higher WHO grade, together with its independence from sex and age. We also observe CLTX binding to intratumoral vasculature in some patients, perhaps preferentially to expanding neovasculature.37,38 This CLTX-CAR T cell targeting of tumor vasculature could also contribute to its therapeutic activity. Similarly, MMP-2 expression on fibroblasts and myeloid cells in the tumor microenvironment39,40,41,42,43 could also be therapeutically beneficial; or, conversely, it could compromise the antitumor efficiency of CTLX-CAR T cells by driving T cell exhaustion. Further studies are required to characterize CLTX binding across these cell types and assess its functional consequences, particularly in relation to stromal and myeloid components of the tumors. Importantly, however, we have previously shown that membrane-associated MMP-2 is associated with CLTX-CAR T cell activation and that soluble MMP-2, potentially secreted in the tumor microenvironment,44,45 neither activates nor disrupts CLTX-CAR function.22 Together these findings support the utility of using MMP-2 immunoreactivity as a surrogate marker for accessibility to CLTX-CAR T cell immunotherapy, therefore overcoming challenges associated with implementing a peptide-binding assay in clinical pathology laboratories.

In this small initial cohort of participants, the clinical benefit mediated by CLTX-CAR T cells cannot be determined, and participants unfortunately did not survive beyond 6 months following treatment. Nevertheless, there are several indications of CLTX-CAR T cell bioactivity. In this initial cohort, a DCR of 75% was observed, with the majority of the participants achieving transient stable disease. Additionally, similar to our clinical experience with IL13Rα2-CAR therapy,2 CLTX-CAR T cells persisted in the tumor cavity and induced locoregional increases in inflammatory cytokines.

One individual of interest (UPN 487), who had multifocal GBM, showed no evidence of tumor progression at the site of CAR T cell administration for over 9 weeks, possibly suggestive of local control of tumor recurrence. This participant instead progressed at a distant site, and the recurrence after CLTX-CAR T cell treatment retained MMP-2 positivity, suggesting either inefficient trafficking of ICT-delivered CAR T cells or suboptimal CAR T cell effector function in the hostile tumor microenvironment. To address potential deficits in trafficking and based on our clinical experience with IL13Rα2-CAR T cell therapy,2 additional cohorts on this ongoing trial will test the utility of dual ICT and intraventricular (ICV) delivery, in which CAR T cells are also administered to the CSF via the lateral ventricle. Based on our preclinical and clinical experience, this dual delivery approach is potentially advantageous, with ICV delivery being effective for treating multifocal tumors and the ICT route beneficial against unifocal tumors. The findings also motivate continuing with dose escalation in this ongoing trial to potentially overcome the suppressive tumor microenvironment.

The therapeutic activity of CLTX-CAR T cells could potentially have been limited by the immunogenicity of this non-human tumor targeting domain. To test for patient antibody reactions to the CLTX-CAR, we developed an antibody-based binding assay employing CAR-engineered reporter cell lines to probe for CAR-specific IgG1 in TCF and serum. Results from this cell-based analytical strategy support the non-immunogenicity of CLTX-CAR T cells in this first cohort of participants. This observation is well aligned with our CAR T cell persistence data showing the continuous presence of CAR T cells in TCF. It is important to note that IgG1 is the most prevalent human IgG subtype and thus would be expected to serve as key indicator of an immune response triggered by CAR T cells. Immunogenicity assays like these will be continued as we follow through with the dual ICT/ICV delivery and dose escalation plan on this ongoing trial.

While a future report describing the results of the full trial upon completion is anticipated, the current findings have also motivated the further development of the CLTX-CAR T cell therapy, and we are currently exploring avenues to potentially increase the potency of the CLTX-CAR T cells. These strategies include possible modifications to the peptide ligand (which is presently the unmodified CLTX sequence), the CAR backbone, and the T cells themselves. Furthermore, combination therapy strategies to support CLTX-CAR T cell persistence and efficacy are also under consideration. These include conditioning with either lymphodepletion or radiation, addition of checkpoint inhibitors, and/or engineering the CAR T cells for transforming growth factor β resistance.

Recent years have seen increased use of toxins in biomedicine, taking advantage of the specificity imparted by predator-prey coevolution. Incorporating toxins into this class of immunotherapy presents an opportunity to enhance the efficacy of other biologically active toxins, such as the anemone toxin targeting Kv1.3, that are already employed as free-standing agents.46 These are agents optimized for high-affinity binding to enhance specificity in clinical use. However, as high affinity confers low intra-tissue mobility, as has been seen with CLTX,15 incorporating these peptides into cells with intrinsic directed motility such as T cells adds to their anti-cancer potential. This is a paradigm shift in immunotherapy focusing specifically on a distinct class of CAR recognition structures and one we suggest should be further explored.

sec.title: Limitations of the study
sec.p: The principal limitation of this interim report on our ongoing clinical trial is the small sample size, as only four patients were evaluated in this arm of the study, limiting our conclusions of clinical utility at this early stage. We will present more comprehensive data and analysis upon completion of this phase 1 clinical trial.

sec.title: Experimental model and study participant details
sec.p: The four participants with recurrent GBM described in this report consisted of three females and one male, ages 40 to 58 years. Karnofsky Performance status (KPS) ranged from 80-90%, and previous treatments included radiation and temozolomide as well as other therapies as indicated in Table 1; however, the patients did not undergo lymphodepleting chemotherapy prior to administration of the CAR T cells.

sec.title: Inclusion and exclusion criteria
sec.p: Enrollment criteria included: age ≥18 years; diagnosis of progressive/recurrent grade 4 malignant glioma; ≥20% moderate/high MMP-2+ tumor expression by IHC ; KPS ≥ 60; life expectancy of > 4-weeks; no known contraindications to leukapheresis, steroids or tocilizumab ; adequate organ function, including white blood cell count >2,000/dL (or absolute neutrophil cell count ≥1,000/μL), platelets ≥100,000/μL, hemoglobin ≥8g/dL, total bilirubin ≤ 1.5x upper limits of normal, alanine transaminase and aspartate transaminase <2.5x upper limits of normal, serum creatinine ≤1.6 mg/dL, oxygen saturation ≥95% and seronegative for HIV Ag/Ab combo; negative pregnancy test in women of childbearing potential and use of adequate contraception in participants of child-bearing potential. Sex was not considered in the study design as GBM occurs in both males and females.

Exclusion criteria included: within 3 months of having received prior bevacizumab; uncontrolled seizure activity and/or clinically evident progressive encephalopathy; history of allergic reactions attributed to compounds of similar chemical or biologic composition to study agent; clinically significant uncontrolled illness; active infection requiring antibiotics; known history of immunodeficiency virus (HIV) or hepatitis B or hepatitis C infection; another active malignancy; females only: pregnant or breastfeeding; any other condition that would contraindicate participation due to safety concerns with clinical study procedures; and inability to comply with all study procedures including compliance issues related to feasibility or logistics.

sec.title: Study design
sec.p: The four participants with recurrent GBM described in this report were treated with CLTX-CAR T on this phase I study between April 2020 and May 2021 (ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT04214392). This study was conducted in accordance with the Institutional Review Board, Data Safety Monitoring Committee, and Independent Ethics Committee at the City of Hope (COH) National Medical Center, as well as the U.S. Food and Drug Administration. All participants provided written informed consent in accordance with local regulatory review. Participants were not compensated for their participation on the study.

Upon enrollment, research participants were assigned a unique patient number (UPN), and their PBMC were collected at the COH Donor Apheresis Center for CAR T cell manufacture. Following radiographic evidence of progression, research subjects then underwent a stereotactic biopsy or resection followed by placement of a Rickham catheter in or proximal to the MRI-defined tumor site (ICT). Following surgery and within 1-2 weeks prior to the first CAR T cell infusion, research subjects underwent baseline MRI and FDG-PET imaging. On the morning of each T cell infusion, the CLTX-CAR T cells were thawed, washed, and reformulated in 0.5 mL preservative-free normal saline (PFNS)/2% human serum albumin (HSA) and delivered manually using a syringe to inject into the Rickham catheter. This was followed by a 0.5 mL PFNS flush over approximately 5 minutes through the Rickham catheter. Note that CAR T cells were administered without prior lymphodepleting chemotherapy.

Participants were deemed evaluable for dose escalation if they received 80% of each of their assigned 3 weekly infusions and were followed for one additional week (i.e., they received 3 cycles of CAR-T cells in the DLT period).

sec.title: Toxicity evaluation
sec.p: Toxicities reported here are limited to those that attributed to protocol therapy. Toxicities were followed at least twice a week during the 28-day DLT period. After the DLT period, participants were followed for worst grade toxicities monthly, then every 3 months for the first year and yearly thereafter. Adverse events were graded according to the CTCAE v5.0, as well as the revised CRS grading system and the modified neurological grading system. DLTs were defined as any grade 3 toxicity (including CRS, neurotoxicity and autoimmune reaction) lasting > 72 hours that was probably or definitely attributed to CAR T cell infusion; or any grade 4 or higher adverse event that was possibly, probably or definitely attributed to CAR T cell infusion; or any attributed toxicity that caused a 2 week delay between two consecutive CAR T infusion cycles. Participants were imaged to assess disease response using modified RANO criteria at the end of the DLT period and every 2-3 months thereafter as clinically indicated.

Participants could continue receiving CAR-T cell infusions at a rate no more frequent than once a week and at ≤ the highest tolerated cell dose in the initial dose schedule, provided that the participant continued to meet eligibility criteria and there were cell doses available from the already manufactured cell product.

sec.title: Participant sample processing
sec.p: Tumor resection material was collected through the COH Department of Pathology according to the clinical protocol. Peripheral blood samples were collected in vacutainer tubes ±EDTA. Samples with EDTA underwent Ficoll-Paque separation immediately upon receipt and peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC) were frozen in CryoStor CS5 at -80°C, followed by transfer to liquid nitrogen for long term storage. Samples without EDTA were allowed to coagulate for 2-3 hours at room temperature; serum was collected by centrifugation, aliquoted in single use 100-200 μL aliquots and stored at -80°C. TCF was collected from the ICT reservoir, spun down, and cell-free supernatants were aliquoted and stored at -80°C. The TCF cells were resuspended in Ca2+/Mg2+-free HBSS (Corning CellGro) with 2% FCS and sodium azide for immediate flow cytometric analysis as described below, with the remaining cells resuspended and frozen in CryoStor CS5 at -80°C and then transferred to liquid nitrogen for long term storage.

sec.title: Imaging
sec.p: Post-gadolinium T1 weighted magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) sequences of the brain and spine were acquired on a Siemens Viro 3 Tesla scanner. Tumor foci were measured on axial T1 MPR weighted images obtained after administration of Multihance (gadobenate dimeglumine). Imaging with 18-F-fluorodeoxyglucose (18-F-FDG) was performed using a GE Discovery DST HP60 PET-CT scanner (70 cm axial field of view, slice thickness 3.75mm). Response assessment was recorded using the modified RANO criteria for GBM.

sec.title: Generation of CLTX-CAR T cells
sec.p: The codon optimized CAR sequence contains a membrane-tethered 36 amino acid CLTX sequence as a binding domain, a human IgG4 Fc spacer containing two mutations (L235E; N297Q) that prevents Fc receptor-mediated recognition,47 a human CD4 transmembrane domain, a human costimulatory 4-1BB cytoplasmic signaling domain, and a human CD3ζ cytoplasmic signaling domain. A T2A ribosome skip sequence48 then separates this CLTX-CAR sequence from a truncated human CD19 sequence (CD19t), an inert, nonimmunogenic cell surface marker. Details for the generation of the lentiviral vector encoding the CLTX-CAR and the CD19t transgene are available upon request.

For CLTX-CAR T cell manufacturing, Tn/mem cells were selected from leukapheresis-derived participant PBMC, stimulated and transduced and expanded as previously described2 using clinical grade CLTX(EQ)28ζ-T2A-CD19t_epHIV7 containing lentivirus22 at an MOI of 0.3 for transduction. Overall, this manufacturing process was completed in 10+ days. Quality control tests on freshly thawed cells included viability, potency (CD19t expression), identity (CD3 expression), CAR identity (qPCR), transgene copy number (WPRE analysis by qPCR), replication competent virus testing (VSV-G analysis by qPCR), residual bead count, and sterility including mycoplasma and endotoxin testing. Cell products were further analyzed by flow cytometry as described below.

sec.title: Immunohistochemistry (IHC)
sec.p: MMP-2 IHC was originally performed on Ventana Discovery Ultra IHC autostainer (Ventana Medical Systems, Roche Diagnostics) using the Discovery ChromoMap DAB Kit (Ventana). After enrollment of the participants described here, the IHC procedure was transferred from the COH Research pathology lab to the COH CLIA lab, where the BenchMark ULTRA IHC/ISH System (Roche Diagnostics) and OptiView DAB IHC Detection Kit (Ventana) were used, and the primary anti-MMP-2 rabbit antibody dilution was switched from 1:100 (original) to 1:50 (updated). All MMP-2 IHC images in Figure 1C depict staining that used the updated assay, except for the UPN 479 tumor at Enrollment, because the same paraffin block for this participant’s tumor was not available to restain and confirm expression with the updated assay.

The anti-human MMP-2 rabbit monoclonal antibody was purchased from Cell Signaling Technology (clone: D4M2N, #40994, RRID: AB_2799191), as suggested by the study principal investigator and pathologist. A glioblastoma (GBM) tumor array including both normal tissue and tumor samples, as reviewed by the study pathologist, was used as a positive control for antibody optimization and staining. FFPE tissue blocks were sectioned at a thickness of 5 μm and placed on positively charged glass slides. After deparaffinization, rehydration, and inhibition of endogenous peroxidase activity, the slides were incubated with a Tris based conditioning reagent (CC1; Ventana) (pH 8.5, 100°C, 32 min) for antigen retrieval, then with anti-MMP-2 (37°C, 1:100 or 1:50 dilution as described above, 32 min), followed by incubation with either the Discovery ChromoMap DAB Kit (Ventana) or OptiView DAB Detection kit (Ventana) as described above. The slides were then counterstained with hematoxylin (Ventana) and coverslipped. Tissues were assigned an H score by the neuropathologist based on the following formula: H = (3 × the percentage of strongly staining cells) + (2 × the percentage of moderately staining cells) + (1 × the percentage of weakly staining cells).

sec.title: Immunofluorescence (IF)
sec.p: Immunofluorescence was done on 5 μm-thick sections of FFPE specimens placed on positively charged glass slides. The slides were deparaffinized in xylene, rehydrated in an ethanol gradient, and underwent antigen retrieval (10 min, 110-116°C) in citrate-based antigen unmasking solution (#H-3300, Vector Laboratories) using a pressure cooker. The slides were then washed and treated with an endogenous biotin-blocking reagent (#E21390-ThermoFisher Scientific) according to manufacturer’s instructions, followed by a carbohydrate-free blocking solution (#SP-5040, Vector Laboratories) prior to staining. The slides were then incubated with anti-MMP-2 antibody (#40994, RRID: AB_2799191, Cell Signaling Technology; 1:50) and biotinylated CLTX peptide (Alomone Labs; 14 μg/mL) overnight at 4°C, followed by incubation with anti-rabbit secondary antibody (#A10040, RRID: AB_2534016, ThermoFisher Scientific; 1:1000) or streptavidin (#S21374, ThermoFisher Scientific; 1:1000) and Hoechst 33342 (#H3570, ThermoFisher Scientific; 1:500) for 1 hour at room temperature. The stained and coverslipped slides were scanned using a Zeiss LSM900 confocal microscope.

sec.title: Flow cytometry
sec.p: CLTX-CAR T cell products were immunophenotyped for memory and exhaustion markers by flow cytometry using either anti-CD3:FITC (Cat#349201; RRID: AB_400405, BD Biosciences), anti-CD8:PE (#340046, RRID: AB_400005, BD Biosciences), anti-CD4:FITC (340133, RRID: AB_400007, BD Biosciences), anti-CD19:PE-Cy7 (#557835, RRID: AB_396893, BD Biosciences), anti-CD27:PE (#555441, RRID: RRID: AB_395834, BD Pharmingen), anti-CD62L:PE (#341012, RRID: AB_400205,BD Biosciences), anti-CD57:FITC (#555619, RRID: AB_395986, BD Biosciences), anti-LAG3(CD223):FITC (#LS-C344745-100, Lifespan Biosciences), anti-PD1:PE (#12-9969-42, RRID: AB_10736473, ThermoFisher Scientific), anti-TIM3:FITC (#11-3109-42, RRID: RRID: AB_2572488, ThermoFisher Scientific) or their respective isotype controls. Related to Figure S1.

For evaluation of CAR T cell persistence in the TCF, cells were stained with antibodies specific for either CD3:Viogreen (#563109, BD Biosciences), CD8:APC-Cy7 (#348793, BD Biosciences), CD19:PE-Cy7 (#557835, BD Biosciences), or their respective isotype controls.
All samples were acquired on a MACSQuant Analyzer 10 (Miltenyi Biotech) and analyzed with FCS express (7.16.0047) or GraphPad Prism Software (v5).

sec.title: qPCR for CAR-T cell persistence
sec.p: Assessment of CAR-T cell persistence in peripheral blood was determined by quantification of the WPRE region of the lentiviral transgene by qPCR. gDNA was extracted from frozen 0.3 mL aliquots of whole blood and tested for the WPRE copy number by TaqMan qPCR. Average copy numbers are presented if ≥2 of 3 replicates generated a cycle threshold (Ct) value. Participants were measured for WPRE before and at least once after every CAR T cell infusion.

sec.title: Cytokine assay
sec.p: Serum, and tumor cavity fluid (TCF) were collected from the implanted Rickham catheter and analyzed by cytokine bead array at the Clinical Immunobiology Correlative Studies Laboratory (CICSL) at City of Hope using the Human Cytokine 30-Plex Panel kit (Invitrogen) and a FLEXMAP 3D plate reader (Luminex).

sec.title: Human anti-CAR antibody (HACA) assay
sec.p: Mock transduced or CLTX-CAR Jurkat T cells were seeded at 105 cells/well in a 96-well plate. Fc block (#564220, RRID: AB_2728082, BD Pharmingen) (1:20) was added to the cells for 10 min, followed by adding either participant TCF (diluted 1:3) or serum (diluted 1:10), or a biosimilar anti-CD19 antibody (#A2173, Biovision) (4 μg/mL). Cells were then incubated with an anti-IgG1 Fc:Alexa Fluor 488 antibody (#A-10631, RRID: AB_2534050, Invitrogen) (20 μg/mL) for 20 min, followed by staining with anti-CD3:Viogreen (#563109, RRID: AB_2732053, BD Biosciences) and anti-CD4:PerCP (#347324, RRID: AB_400282, BD Biosciences) for appropriate gating strategies. The presence of IgG1 in the samples was assessed using a MACSQuant Analyzer 10 (Miltenyi Biotech), FCS Express software (7.16.0047), and GraphPad Prism Software (v5).

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: DLT and disease response rates were presented with 90% exact binomial confidence intervals. Worst grade toxicities attributed to CAR T cell treatment are presented by AE category. Baseline characteristics are presented per participant. Confidence intervals and toxicity tables were created using R v4.4 (https://www.R-project.org/).

Low dimensional representation of the 30-dimensional cytokine data was obtained by the application of multidimensional scaling (MDS) to the proximity matrix generated by a random forest trained on the data. Density plots were constructed using kernel density estimators with Gaussian kernels and bandwidth estimated through cross-validation.

Upon receiving a request, the lead contact will review the request with COH Clinical & Human Research Protections Program that manages the external distribution of data generated from COH clinical trials. In order to ensure patient privacy, access to personally identifiable information or sensitive clinical information will not be provided, and requests for data access must rigorously adhere to the consent agreements established with study participants.
Any additional information required to reanalyze the data reported in this paper is available from the lead contact upon request.
